note: Raw output of the unmodified probe. Three entries are WRONG as measurements and are corrected below in `corrections` — read that block before trusting mtime/permissions/symlink.

corrections._why: The probe measures three things in ways that do not survive scrutiny on macOS. Each was re-measured with a dedicated experiment; the corrected value replaces the probe field.

mtime_granularity_seconds.method: 200 consecutive rewrites of one file as fast as possible, reading fs.statSync({bigint:true}).mtimeNs each time; counted distinct values and the step size between consecutive distinct ones.
mtime_granularity_seconds.interpretation: exFAT stores mtime in 10 ms units and macOS honors that. 0.25 s was only the probe's own sampling interval (20 writes over 5 s), i.e. a floor imposed by the measurement, not a property of the volume. The 2.000 s figure reported on Windows is therefore a driver behavior, not an exFAT requirement — same spec, two drivers, 200x difference. Reference point: APFS on the same machine gave 200/200 distinct with sub-millisecond steps.

mode_after_chmod_0600.corrected: 0o700 — but chmod is a complete no-op, not an applied 0700
mode_after_chmod_0600.method: write a file, stat mode, then chmod 0600 / 0777 / 0000 in turn, stat after each, and finally try to read the file back.
mode_after_chmod_0600.interpretation: mode is frozen at 0o700 by the mount, so every chmod appears to succeed and does nothing. Verified against APFS on the same machine, where chmod works normally (0o644 -> 0600 -> 0777 -> 0o000, and chmod 000 yields EACCES).

permissions_enforced.reason: FALSE POSITIVE in the probe. It tests `(mode & 0o077) === 0`, which merely asks whether group/other bits are clear. macOS mounts exFAT with `noowners` and reports 0o700 for every file unconditionally, so the test passes without chmod having done anything. This is exactly the failure mode the finding warns about: a check that measures the mount's cosmetic default instead of enforcement.

links.interpretation: macOS can create real, followable symlinks inside an exFAT volume — absolute and relative. So the Windows-side blanket rule 'the volume cannot host a link layout' is false for macOS. Caveat: Windows still cannot create them, so the layout is not portable; and whether Windows can *read* a symlink macOS created on exFAT is UNVERIFIED (no Windows machine in this session).

extra_verification.mount_options: exfat, local, noowners, noatime, fskit — `noowners` is the reason chmod is inert and mode reads 0o700

lsof_can_detect_the_writer.interpretation: lsof +D is a reliable liveness check on this volume and is strictly better than `kill -0`: it names the holder and shows whether a -wal is actually open. Needed because a process can lose its database connection without exiting (see B5).

appledouble_noise.interpretation: Node file operations on this volume did not generate ._* companions; the 9 at the root pre-date the probes (Windows-written items carrying extended attributes). Any directory walk still has to exclude them.

macos_only_traps.trap: Opening a WAL database read-only on the shared volume fails
macos_only_traps.cause: A WAL reader must create / map the -shm file in the same directory. If the directory is not writable (or the volume is mounted read-only), SQLite cannot open the database at all — even though nothing is being written.
macos_only_traps.misleading_because: The error says 'unable to open database file', which reads like 'the file is missing or corrupt' during an incident, when it actually means 'this directory is not writable'.
macos_only_traps.workaround: ?immutable=1 opens without -shm — but immutable=1 tells SQLite the file cannot change, so it IGNORES the WAL entirely. You will then read a stale database and may get 'no such table' for tables that exist only in the WAL. Never use immutable=1 to judge whether data is intact.
macos_only_traps.correct_move: Copy the whole set (state.db + -wal + -shm) to a writable local directory first, then open the copy.

macos_only_traps.trap: A process can close its database without exiting
macos_only_traps.symptom: The writer pid is alive (ps shows state R) yet holds no descriptor on state.db, and -wal/-shm are gone.
macos_only_traps.cause: See B5: V8 garbage-collects the DatabaseSync object once the script no longer references it; node:sqlite closes the connection on finalization, and SQLite then checkpoints and deletes -wal/-shm by contract.
macos_only_traps.consequence: `kill -0` / pid liveness does NOT prove the database is still open. Use `lsof +D <dir>` and look for state.db / state.db-wal.
macos_only_traps.note: The close is clean, so no data is lost — the WAL is checkpointed into the main file first. The trap is the inference, not the data.

b5.verdict: EXPLAINED — not a volume artifact, not a node:sqlite connection-parameter issue
b5.root_cause: V8 GC finalization of the DatabaseSync handle. crash-probe's child performs 500 inserts, writes the signal file, then busy-waits WITHOUT ever touching the handle again. Once the handle is unreachable, GC collects it, node:sqlite closes the connection, and SQLite checkpoints + deletes -wal/-shm — exactly as a clean close would.

variants.A_handle_unused: verbatim crash-probe child; -wal disappeared 3/3 on exFAT, 2/2 on APFS
variants.B_keep_alive: same + `globalThis.__keep = h`; -wal disappeared 0/3 on exFAT, 0/2 on APFS
variants.C_explicit_close: same + explicit h.close(); disk end-state identical to A (db 4096 -> 16384, no -wal/-shm)

ab_test.conclusion: The only variable that matters is whether the JS handle is still referenced. Filesystem, journal_mode, synchronous setting and explicit transactions were all ruled out separately (lab/b5-bisect-style runs: every combination produced -wal = 2,080,632 B with a 4096 B main file while the handle was alive).

what_is_actually_true: While the connection is open, the WAL is real and holds all the data: 500 rows -> -wal = 2,080,632 B, main file still 4,096 B.
A reader with a normal connection sees all 500 rows and journal_mode=wal.
The WAL is checkpointed and removed only when the last connection closes — cleanly or via GC finalization.
A db-only copy taken while a live -wal exists is NOT a valid handoff: it produced 500 rows here only because a checkpoint had already backfilled the main file; do not rely on that.
b5.protocol_consequence: Unchanged and reinforced: never infer anything from the presence, absence, or size of -wal, nor from the main file's size. Trust only your own hash, your own integrity_check, and your own receipt. And use lsof, not pid liveness, to decide whether the writer is really done.
